comparability: Retain three qualified, substantively distinct responses after challenging each from actual content, contribution and weight. Each contains all six available History courses / 45 EC: modern history, American gender history with interviews, empire, warfare, Native American social/cultural history, and a final archival/primary-source research paper on Walcheren 1809. This is sustained historical object/method/progression, not merely a coherent unrelated programme or a generic interest in society. Cultural heritage/public memory adds art/archaeology, historiography, life-writing and historical media; political conflict/social inclusion adds institutions, rights, international relations and sociological enquiry; political economy adds five economic theory/inference courses plus social theory to study mechanisms of historical change. These companions have distinct taught objects/methods and change substantial course weight, not just labels. Their relevance does not make economics, statistics, sociology or contemporary politics into economic/migration history. No UCR composition reproduces VU broader medieval/early-modern and Netherlands sequences, Holocaust-centred genocide historiography, digital-history training, Low Countries devotion research, specialist photography seminar or individual History thesis. Numerical overlap is a feasibility/traceability check, not the comparability argument. Three pass on this basis; no fourth omnibus or generic-method alternative is justified. Two additional candidate directions are explicitly rejected: the illustrative crime-history question (row 4568) does not establish specialist Holocaust/genocide progression in the available UCR courses; migration history (row 4574) has limited support through historical gender/Indigenous inquiry and contemporary inclusion, but lacks a distinct specialist migration-history composition. Their formal registry generator roles remain accounted for through rejected candidates, without authorising another included programme.
